## Why a Flashcard Is Metacognition You Can Hold


**A flashcard works because it forces a prediction you can check.** You read the front, you try to answer, you flip the card, and you see at once whether you knew it. That moment is metacognition: thinking about your own thinking. John Flavell named the field in 1979, and Thomas Nelson and Louis Narens (1990) split it into two jobs, monitoring (how well do I know this?) and control (what do I study next?).


Rereading gives you no such moment. A page you have seen twice feels familiar, and familiarity feels like knowing. Asher Koriat and Robert Bjork (2005) called the result an illusion of competence: when the answer sits in front of you while you study, you overrate how well you will recall it later. A flashcard hides the answer, so the illusion breaks on the first card you miss.


The pink diamond is the whole point. Every card is a small experiment on your own memory, and the rating you give is your monitoring judgment. The spaced repetition app then turns that judgment into control: it decides when you see the card again.


Students already know half of this. In a survey of 472 UCLA undergraduates, Nate Kornell and Robert Bjork (2007, *Psychonomic Bulletin & Review* ) found that most students who tested themselves did it mainly to check what they knew, not because testing itself builds memory. Both reasons are true. A self-test tells you what you do not know, and the act of recall makes the memory stronger. For the full story on how monitoring and control work, read our guide to[what metacognition is](https://www.taskade.com/blog/what-is-metacognition) .


### What AI changes, and what it does not


Step Who does it with an AI flashcard maker Can AI do it for you?


Find the facts worth learning AI drafts, you choose Partly. AI cannot know what your exam stresses


Write the question AI drafts, you edit Yes for a draft, no for the final card


Try to recall the answer You No. This is where learning happens


Judge whether you knew it You No. This is the metacognition


Decide when to review The scheduler Yes. Algorithms do this well


Repair a card you keep missing You, with AI help Partly. AI can suggest a split


The rows marked "You" are the ones no tool can take over. An AI that writes 300 cards in a minute saves the slowest step, but it also tempts you to skip the step that makes cards work: deciding what you need to learn and saying it in your own words.

## The Learning Science Behind Flashcards, in Five Minutes


**Two findings explain why flashcards work: retrieval practice and spacing.** In their 2013 review of ten common study techniques, John Dunlosky and colleagues rated practice testing and distributed practice the only two with high utility. Flashcards with a scheduler combine both. This section is short on purpose. The history and the algorithms are in our guide to[spaced repetition explained](https://www.taskade.com/blog/spaced-repetition-explained) .


### The testing effect


Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke (2006, *Psychological Science* ) had students read prose passages and then either reread them or take a recall test. Rereaders did better at five minutes. Testers did better a week later. The students who reread also felt more confident, which is the illusion of competence again. Karpicke and Roediger (2008, *Science* ) then showed that dropping a learned item from testing hurt later recall, while dropping it from restudy did not.


Two meta-analyses confirm the pattern across hundreds of studies: Christopher Rowland (2014, *Psychological Bulletin* ) and Olusola Adesope, Dominic Trevisan and Narayankripa Sundararajan (2017, *Review of Educational Research* ). Recall beats review.


### The spacing effect


Hermann Ebbinghaus described forgetting and the value of spaced study in 1885. Nicholas Cepeda and colleagues (2006, *Psychological Bulletin* ) reviewed the distributed practice literature and found that spreading study over time beats massing it, for the same total study time. For flashcards the sharpest test is Kornell (2009, *Applied Cognitive Psychology* ):


Finding from Kornell (2009) What it means for your deck


One big stack beat four small stacks A big stack puts more time between repeats of each card


90% of participants learned more with spacing The effect held for almost everyone, not just on average


After the first session, 72% believed massing had worked better Your feeling about what works is not a reliable guide


That last row is the metacognition problem in one number. Cramming feels better while it is happening, so learners pick it, even when it works worse.


### Making your own cards beats premade cards


This is the finding that matters most for AI flashcards. Steven Pan, Inez Zung, Megan Imundo, Xuxin Zhang and Yunning Qiu (2023, *Journal of Applied Research in Memory and Cognition* ) ran six experiments in which students studied text passages with either cards they made themselves or premade cards, and then took a test 48 hours later.


Self-made cards won on definition questions (d = 0.45) and, in most experiments, on application questions (d = 0.29). The authors also report that most participants did not realize how much making the cards helped. An AI-generated deck is a premade deck. The practical rule follows directly: let AI draft the deck, then do the making yourself by editing, rewriting, cutting and adding. The generation effect, first shown by Norman Slamecka and Peter Graf (1978), points the same way: what you produce, you remember better than what you only read.


Research finding Source Rule for AI flashcards


Recall beats rereading on delayed tests Roediger and Karpicke, 2006 Study by answering cards, not by reading the deck


Keep testing items you already got right Karpicke and Roediger, 2008 Do not delete a card after one correct answer


Spaced study beats massed study Cepeda et al., 2006 Use a scheduler, not a night-before marathon


Big stacks beat small stacks Kornell, 2009 Shuffle the whole deck instead of drilling 10 cards


Dropping cards early hurts a little Kornell and Bjork, 2008 Let the scheduler retire cards, not your mood


Self-made cards beat premade cards Pan et al., 2023 Edit and rewrite every AI card


Overconfidence ends study too early Dunlosky and Rawson, 2012 Trust your miss rate, not your feeling

## What Makes a Good Flashcard (and Why AI Often Writes Bad Ones)


**A good flashcard asks for one fact, has one correct answer, and takes a few seconds to answer.** Piotr Wozniak, who created SuperMemo, wrote this down in 1999 as rule 4 of his[twenty rules of formulating knowledge](https://www.supermemo.com/en/blog/twenty-rules-of-formulating-knowledge) : stick to the minimum information principle. AI tools break this rule more than any other, because a language model likes to write complete, paragraph-sized answers.


### The minimum information principle


A card that asks for five facts at once fails in a hidden way. You remember three, you feel you mostly know it, you rate it "good," and the two weak facts never get the extra reviews they need. Split the card, and each fact gets its own schedule.


### Bad cards and better cards


These are the five card shapes AI tools produce most often, with the rewrite for each.


Bad card an AI tends to write Problem Better card


"Explain the causes of World War I." Essay, not a card "Whose assassination in June 1914 triggered the July Crisis?"


"List the 7 SI base units." A set to enumerate Seven cards, one per unit: "What is the SI base unit of electric current?"


"What is photosynthesis?" with a 60-word answer Too much on the back "Which gas do plants take in during photosynthesis?"


"Mitochondria are important because ___." Many correct answers "Which organelle makes most of the cell's ATP?"


"True or false: enzymes are proteins." Guessable, half right "Enzymes are mostly made of which class of molecule?"


### Cloze deletion: the card format AI handles best


A cloze card hides one word or phrase inside a sentence. Wozniak's rule 5 reads "Cloze deletion is easy and effective," and Anki has a[built-in cloze note type](https://docs.ankiweb.net/editing.html) . It suits AI well because the source sentence stays intact, so the tool cannot drift far from the text. In Anki the syntax looks like this:


```text
The {{c1::mitochondrion}} makes most of the cell's ATP.
Aspirin irreversibly inhibits {{c1::cyclooxygenase (COX)}} enzymes.
The Treaty of {{c1::Westphalia}} ended the Thirty Years' War in {{c2::1648}}.


```


The third line makes two cards from one sentence, one for the treaty and one for the year. That is fine, because each card still asks for one fact.


### Card types and when to use each


Subject Best card type Example front


Vocabulary and languages Reversible "el perro" and, on its own card, "the dog"


Medicine and biology Cloze and image occlusion A labeled diagram of the heart with one label hidden


History and law Basic, with dates as cloze "Which case established judicial review in the US?"


Math and physics Basic, with a worked step "What is the first step to solve a quadratic by completing the square?"


Programming Basic, with a code snippet "What does this one-line list comprehension return?"


Concepts and theory Why or how prompts "Why does a vaccine produce memory cells?"


### Wozniak's rules, applied to AI drafts


Five of the twenty rules do most of the work when you edit an AI deck:


Rule (Wozniak, 1999) What to check in an AI draft


1. Do not learn if you do not understand Delete any card you cannot explain. Learn the idea first, then card it


4. Stick to the minimum information principle Split any answer longer than one short line


9 and 10. Avoid sets and avoid enumerations Break every "list the" card into single facts


11. Combat interference Add a cue when two cards look alike, for example the chapter name


18. Provide sources Keep the page number or video time on the back


Here is the anatomy of a card that passes all five checks:


```text
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
| FRONT                                                       |
|   [Pharmacology, Ch. 4]                       <- cue / tag  |
|   Aspirin irreversibly inhibits which enzymes?              |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
| BACK                                                        |
|   Cyclooxygenase (COX-1 and COX-2)            <- one fact   |
|   Source: lecture slides p. 23                <- source     |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
| CHECKS: one fact | one answer | under 10 seconds | sourced  |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+


```


If you want to understand an idea before you card it, the[Feynman technique](https://www.taskade.com/blog/feynman-technique) is the natural first pass: explain it in plain words from memory, find the gaps, then turn each repaired gap into a card.

## How AI Flashcard Makers Work


**Every AI flashcard maker runs the same four steps: extract the text, find the facts, write question and answer pairs, and hand you a draft.** The quality differences come from step two, choosing what matters, and from how easy the tool makes step four, your edit.


Three limits follow from this pipeline:


- **YouTube tools read the transcript, not the picture.** If a lecturer points at a diagram and says "this one here," no card will capture the diagram. A video without captions gives the tool nothing to read.
- **Scanned PDFs need OCR.** A photo of a page is an image until something reads the letters. Check the first cards from a scanned file against the page.
- **AI picks what is easy to card, not what is on your exam.** Definitions get carded first because they are easy to spot. The worked problem your professor stressed may never appear. Tell the tool what to focus on.


For a deeper look at the reading step, our guides to[PDF to notes AI tools](https://www.taskade.com/blog/pdf-to-notes) ,[YouTube to notes tools](https://www.taskade.com/blog/youtube-to-notes) and[handwritten notes to text apps](https://www.taskade.com/blog/handwritten-notes-ai) compare how each type of tool extracts text.

## 2. Anki: Best Free Review Engine (Add AI With an Add-On)


**Anki is the free, open flashcard app that many medical students and language learners use for long-term review, and it now ships the FSRS scheduler built in.** It writes no cards with AI by itself. You add AI through an add-on or import cards that another tool wrote.


**What it is.**[Anki](https://apps.ankiweb.net/) runs on Windows, macOS and Linux, with AnkiDroid on Android and AnkiMobile on iOS. The current desktop release on the download page is 26.09.4. The desktop app, AnkiDroid and AnkiWeb sync are free. AnkiMobile is a paid app, and its purchases fund development.


**How it makes cards.** You type them, import them, or use an add-on. Anki has a[built-in cloze note type](https://docs.ankiweb.net/editing.html) , and since version 23.10 it supports image occlusion cards natively. Its[text importer](https://docs.ankiweb.net/importing/text-files.html) reads files separated by commas or tabs, which is how cards from ChatGPT, Taskade and most AI tools get in. Add-ons on AnkiWeb add AI. One example, the open-source Anki AI field generator, fills fields on cards you already have using your own AI provider key. Another, NovaCards, generates cloze cards from pasted notes or uploaded PDF, DOCX and PPTX files and adds them to your collection.


**Free plan.** Everything except AnkiMobile is free. Add-ons that call an AI provider can need your own paid API key.


**Pros:**


- The[FSRS scheduler](https://docs.ankiweb.net/deck-options.html) lets you set a target, with a default desired retention of 90%.
- Cloze, image occlusion, audio, images and add-ons cover almost any subject.
- Your collection is yours, and huge shared decks exist for medicine and languages.


**Cons:**


- No native AI card writer. AI means add-ons, imports and setup.
- The interface takes time to learn.
- AnkiMobile on iOS costs money.


**Pricing.** Free on desktop, Android and web. AnkiMobile is a paid app.


**Best for.** Anyone who studies for months or years, such as medical boards, bar exams and languages, and wants the strongest scheduler. Pair it with an AI tool for the first draft.

## 3. Quizlet: Best for Fast Sets and a Huge Shared Library


**Quizlet turns pasted text, a PDF, slides, a Word file or a Google Drive document into a draft flashcard set with its Smart Assist feature, and its Learn mode adapts questions to what you know.** It is the most familiar name in flashcards, with a large library of public sets.


**What it is.**[Quizlet](https://quizlet.com/) is a study platform with flashcards, Learn, practice tests and study guides on the web, iOS and Android.


**How it makes cards.** In the help center steps, you select Create, start a flashcard set, then type or paste text, upload a file, or enter a topic. Smart Assist writes draft cards in a preview where you can edit, delete or add before you publish. Quizlet lists PDF, PowerPoint and Word files as inputs, up to 100,000 characters of pasted text in one session, and Google Drive as a source.


**Free plan.** You can make sets by hand and use core study modes. Some AI features are free with limited access. Learn is free for a limited number of rounds per set, and Plus subscribers get more.


**Pros:**


- The draft preview makes editing before you study easy.
- A large library of public sets for common courses.
- Learn mode mixes question types and adapts to your answers.


**Cons:**


- Heavier AI use and full Learn access sit behind a paid plan.
- Quizlet does not describe Learn as a spaced repetition algorithm.
- Public sets are premade cards, with the weaker results Pan and colleagues found.


**Pricing.** Quizlet sells two paid plans, Quizlet Plus and Plus Unlimited. Quizlet's upgrade page blocked our check on November 10, 2026, so we leave the prices out. Check the upgrade page before you buy.


**Best for.** Students who want a set in a minute, who study with classmates on Quizlet already, or who want a public set for a standard course to adapt.


---


## 4. Knowt: Best Free Study System Built Around Flashcards


**Knowt is the free Quizlet alternative that makes flashcards from files with its AI, Kai, and gives free Learn and spaced repetition modes.** It has one of the most generous free tiers among the AI flashcard apps we compared.


**What it is.**[Knowt](https://knowt.com/) is a study app on the web and on mobile with flashcards, notes, practice tests and AP, SAT and ACT prep.


**How it makes cards.** The[AI flashcard maker](https://knowt.com/ai-flashcard-maker) page lists PDFs, images, videos, slides and audio, plus Google Drive and YouTube, with up to 30 files at once. "Kai will make flashcards instantly," the page says. Knowt says its Chrome extension imports Quizlet flashcards in two clicks, with images and formatting.


**Free plan.** Knowt's FAQ says you can make AI flashcards for free. Its[Learn mode](https://knowt.com/learn-mode) is free for every set, any number of times, and Knowt says its spaced repetition mode is free too.


**Pros:**


- Learn and spaced repetition are free, not trial features.
- Many study modes from one set: Learn, practice test, spaced repetition, match and more.
- A simple path from Quizlet with the Chrome extension.


**Cons:**


- The plans page does not say which AI limits apply on Free.
- Many features to learn if you only want a deck.
- Ultra is expensive month to month.


**Pricing.** Ultra is $7.99 a month billed as $95.99 a year, or $24.99 billed monthly. Ultra adds AI summarizers for PDFs, videos and slides, a lecture recording summarizer and more.


**Best for.** Students who want a full free study system around flashcards, and anyone leaving Quizlet.


---


## 5. RemNote: Best for Notes and Flashcards in One App


**RemNote is a note-taking app where flashcards grow out of your notes, with AI that turns text, PDFs and YouTube videos into cards and a built-in spaced repetition schedule.** It is the pick when you want one app, not a notes app plus a flashcard app.


**What it is.**[RemNote](https://www.remnote.com/) is a notes and spaced repetition app for the web, desktop and mobile. You write a note, mark parts as flashcards, and review them on a schedule.


**How it makes cards.** You can turn a line of notes into a card as you type. AI "Text to Cards" turns pasted text into cards.[YouTube to Cards](https://www.remnote.com/youtube_to_cards) extracts the main ideas of a video into cards that stay in RemNote, and you can edit them and add exam dates. The pricing page lists "Learn PDF: AI Flashcards, Quizzes, and Summaries" on the Pro with AI plan.


**Free plan.** Free includes 5 AI cards and 250 AI credits a month. You can start YouTube to Cards for free.


**Pros:**


- Cards stay linked to the note they came from, so context is one click away.
- Exam dates on cards fit review to a deadline.
- Making cards while you take notes is a natural self-made workflow.


**Cons:**


- The free AI allowance is small.
- The full PDF flashcard feature sits on the most expensive plan.
- The annual plan shows no discount over monthly on the pricing page.


**Pricing.** Pro is $8 a month or $96 a year. Pro with AI is $18 a month or $216 a year, with 1,000 AI cards and 20,000 AI credits a month.


**Best for.** Students who take notes in one app and want flashcards to grow out of them, especially in theory-heavy courses.


---


## 6. Gizmo: Best for Game-Style Review


**Gizmo turns PDFs, YouTube videos, notes and slides into AI flashcards and quizzes, then reviews them in a game-style Memorise mode that uses spaced repetition.** It is built to make review feel like a game.


**What it is.**[Gizmo](https://gizmo.ai/) is an AI quiz and flashcard app, with the tagline "Get addicted to learning."


**How it makes cards.** The site lists PDF to Flashcards, YouTube to Flashcards, Notes to Flashcards and PowerPoint to Flashcards. Its Magic Import accepts PDFs, recordings, pasted notes, photos, PowerPoint, Quizlet sets, existing Anki decks and CSV files. After import, Gizmo highlights key words, and those are what Memorise mode quizzes you on.


**Free plan.** Free works, with a 20-minute wait between imports, per Gizmo's help center. The Unlimited plan removes the wait.


**Pros:**


- Memorise mode uses spaced repetition to pick when each card returns.
- Many question types: multiple choice with AI-written wrong options, typing, voice, matching, true or false and ordering.
- Imports both Anki decks and Quizlet sets, so you can bring old decks.


**Cons:**


- Multiple choice with AI distractors tests recognition, which is easier than recall.
- The import wait slows a big batch on Free.
- Prices are not listed on the pages we could read.


**Pricing.** Free and Unlimited plans. Gizmo's public pages did not show a price when we checked, so we leave the number out.


**Best for.** Students who skip review because it feels like a chore, and groups that want live multiplayer quizzes with Gizmo Live.

## 7. Gemini Notebook (Formerly NotebookLM): Best for Cards Grounded in Your Sources


**Gemini Notebook, the new name for Google's NotebookLM since July 16, 2026, generates flashcards from the sources you upload to a notebook, with difficulty and quantity settings.** Its cards stay tied to your own material, not to the open web.


**What it is.**[Gemini Notebook](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/products/gemini-notebook/notebooklm-gemini-notebook/) is Google's research notebook. You add sources such as PDFs, docs and links, then ask questions or generate study aids from them. Google's announcement says it remains a standalone product and also connects to the Gemini app.


**How it makes cards.** Per the[help center](https://support.google.com/notebooklm/answer/16958963?hl=en) , open the Studio panel and select Flashcards. The pencil icon lets you pick easy, medium or hard, choose fewer, standard or more cards, and add a prompt for focus, style or audience. You mark each card "Got it!" or "Missed it!", and you can retry only the cards you missed. An Explain button explains a card, you can delete a card from the deck, and you can download the deck as a CSV file.


**Free plan.** Flashcards work in the free product. Usage limits apply, and Google lists them on a separate page.


**Pros:**


- Cards come from your own sources, which cuts invented facts.
- "Only cards you missed" is a quick self-test loop.
- CSV download makes the deck easy to move to Anki.


**Cons:**


- No spaced repetition schedule.
- Limited control over individual card wording compared with a full editor.
- Built for research first, so deck management is basic.


**Pricing.** Free to use, within the usage limits that Google lists on its help center.


**Best for.** Students who already keep course readings in a notebook and want quick, grounded cards to export into a scheduler.

## 8. StudyFetch: Best for Cards With Citations to the Source


**StudyFetch turns PDFs, slides, documents, lecture recordings, images of notes and YouTube links into flashcards, quizzes and games, and every flashcard cites the part of your material it came from.** That citation makes checking an AI card fast.


**What it is.**[StudyFetch](https://www.studyfetch.com/) is an AI study platform with a tutor called Sparky, a Live Lecture recorder and an Arcade of study games.


**How it makes cards.** You upload your own material or paste a YouTube link. The homepage says every flashcard "comes with citations back to your original materials." Live Lecture records a class and turns it into study material.


**Free plan.** "Getting started with StudyFetch is free," the homepage says. Premium is described for students who want it as their full study system.


**Pros:**


- Citations on every card make the accuracy check quick.

## How a Card Moves Through a Spaced Repetition Scheduler


**A spaced repetition scheduler moves each card from new to learning to review, and it stretches the gap every time you recall the card.** In Anki, a card with an interval of 21 days or more counts as mature. If you forget a card, it lapses and goes through relearning before its gaps start to grow again. This diagram shows the forward path.


This is why the source of your cards matters more than the speed of the generator. A scheduler can only space what you give it. A deck of vague, multi-fact cards gets scheduled just as faithfully as a deck of sharp ones, and you pay for the vague ones every day.


Most decks share one data shape, whichever tool you use:


Keep the SOURCE link on every card, either a page number or a video time. When a card turns out to be wrong, the source tells you where to check.

## Workflow 1: PDF to Flashcards in Four Steps


**To create flashcards from a PDF, generate a draft from one chapter at a time, edit every card, add the page number, and then move the deck to your review tool.** The edit step is not optional. It is where a premade deck becomes a self-made one.


### Step 1: Generate a draft from one chapter


Open the[PDF to Flashcards converter](https://www.taskade.com/convert/pdf/pdf-to-flashcards) and import one chapter, not the whole textbook. A smaller input gives the AI less room to wander and gives you a deck you can edit in one sitting. In Taskade the cards land in a project as question and answer pairs. For slide decks, use[Presentation to Flashcards](https://www.taskade.com/convert/presentation/presentation-to-flashcards) .


### Step 2: Tell the AI what matters


Paste your syllabus line, the learning objectives at the top of the chapter, or your professor's review sheet, and ask for cards on those points only. Here is a prompt that works in any of the tools above:


```text
Make flashcards from the attached chapter for my exam on [topic].
Rules:
- One fact per card. The answer must fit on one short line.
- Write questions that have exactly one correct answer.
- Turn every list into separate cards, one item each.
- Use cloze format for definitions: "The {{c1::term}} is ...".
- Add the page number on the back of every card.
- Skip examples, anecdotes and anything not in the objectives below.
Objectives: [paste the learning objectives]
Output a two-column table: Front | Back.


```


### Step 3: Edit until the deck is yours


Go through every card and ask four questions: is it one fact, does it have one answer, can I answer it in a few seconds, and do I understand it? Delete what fails, split what is too big, and rewrite the rest in your own words. This is the step that the Pan et al. results reward.


### Step 4: Move the deck into your review habit


If you review in Taskade, ask the agent to quiz you and to mark missed cards. If you want strict long-term spacing, export the project as a CSV file, check that front and back sit in separate columns, and import the file into Anki. For a broader plan around the deck, the[PDF to Study Guide converter](https://www.taskade.com/convert/pdf/pdf-to-study-guide) and[PDF to Notes converter](https://www.taskade.com/convert/pdf/pdf-to-notes) build the other half of the study kit, and our guide to[AI study guide makers](https://www.taskade.com/blog/ai-study-guide-makers) compares the rest.

## Common Mistakes With AI Flashcards


**The most common mistake is generating 500 cards and studying none of them.** A deck you never review teaches nothing, however good the cards are. The other mistakes are subtler, and each one has a direct fix.


Mistake What happens Fix


Generating the whole textbook at once A huge deck you never finish One chapter or lecture at a time


Studying AI cards without editing Premade-card results Edit, rewrite and cut every card


Cards with long answers You half-know them and rate them "good" One fact per card


Deleting a card after one correct answer Weaker long-term recall Let the scheduler retire cards


Drilling 10 cards until they feel easy Massed practice that feels better than it works Shuffle the whole deck, review daily


Trusting the AI on numbers A wrong dose, date or formula gets memorized Check every number against the source


Only multiple-choice review You practice recognition, not recall Type or say the answer before you flip


Never rewriting a card you keep missing The same lapse every week Split it or add a cue

## Frequently Asked Questions About AI Flashcard Makers


What is the best AI flashcard maker in 2026?


It depends on how you review. Anki is the strongest free review engine, with the FSRS scheduler built in, but it needs an add-on or another tool to write cards with AI. Quizlet and Knowt build a set from notes or a PDF in seconds. RemNote keeps notes and cards in one app. Taskade turns a PDF, slides, a YouTube link or pasted notes into an editable deck inside the same workspace as your notes, study plan and study group.


Is there a free AI flashcard maker?


Yes, with limits. Knowt says its AI flashcard maker is free, and its Learn mode and spaced repetition mode are free. Gemini Notebook, formerly NotebookLM, makes flashcards from your sources. RemNote Free includes a small number of AI cards. Brainscape Free lets you make hundreds of cards with AI. Anki is free on desktop and Android, but its AI comes from add-ons. On Taskade Free, you earn free AI credits with referrals and invites, and you can upgrade any time.


How do I turn a PDF into flashcards with AI?


Upload the PDF to an AI flashcard maker, pick the pages or chapter you need, and generate a first draft. Then edit every card: one fact per card, a question you can answer in a few seconds, and the page number as the source. Delete the cards you do not need. In Taskade, the[PDF to Flashcards converter](https://www.taskade.com/convert/pdf/pdf-to-flashcards) turns the file into question and answer pairs in a project you can edit and share. PDF upload needs a paid plan.


Can AI make flashcards from a YouTube video?


Yes, if the video has captions or a transcript. Most tools read the transcript, not the picture, so a diagram that is never said out loud does not become a card. Taskade imports a YouTube link into a project with AI, and its YouTube to Anki converter drafts cloze or question cards from the transcript. RemNote, Knowt, Gizmo and StudyFetch also accept YouTube links.


Can AI make Anki cards?


Yes, in two ways. An Anki add-on can write or fill cards inside Anki, and some add-ons need your own AI provider key. Or another tool writes the cards and you import them, because Anki imports text files separated by commas or tabs. Anki has no AI card writer built in, but it has cloze deletion, image occlusion and the FSRS scheduler.


Are AI-generated flashcards as good as cards you make yourself?


Not by default. Pan and colleagues (2023, Journal of Applied Research in Memory and Cognition) found across six experiments that students who made their own flashcards scored better on a test 48 hours later than students who used premade cards, with an effect size of d = 0.45 on definition questions. An AI deck is a premade deck, so edit, rewrite and cut it until the cards are yours.


What makes a good flashcard?


A good flashcard asks for one fact, has one correct answer, and can be answered in a few seconds. Piotr Wozniak of SuperMemo called this the minimum information principle. Use cloze deletion for facts inside a sentence, split lists into single cards, add the source page, and rewrite any card you keep getting wrong instead of just repeating it.


Can I study Taskade flashcards with spaced repetition?


Yes, in two ways. The AI Flashcard Tutor agent quizzes you and brings missed cards back more often, and a scheduled automation can send you a daily review list. Taskade does not run an algorithmic scheduler such as FSRS. For long-term spaced repetition across months, export the deck as a CSV file and import it into Anki.


Can ChatGPT make flashcards?


Yes. ChatGPT can write question and answer pairs from pasted text or an uploaded file, and its study mode adds knowledge checks and hints. It has no dedicated flashcard deck or review scheduler, so most people ask it for a two-column table and import the result into Anki, Quizlet or another app. Long documents work better one chapter at a time.


What is Gemini Notebook, and can it make flashcards?


Gemini Notebook is the new name of NotebookLM, which Google announced on July 16, 2026. In the Studio panel you can generate flashcards from your sources, pick easy, medium or hard, mark each card Got it or Missed it, practice only the cards you missed, and download the deck as a CSV file.


Which AI flashcard maker is best for medical students?


Many medical students review in Anki because of cloze deletion, image occlusion, add-ons and the FSRS scheduler. AI helps with the first draft. An add-on or a tool such as Taskade, RemNote or Knowt writes cloze cards from lecture slides, and the student edits and imports them. Check every drug, dose and number against the source.
